summary: A verifiable credential is a signed statement made by one party about a subject that a third party can check without asking the first party. The data model became a full web recommendation on 15 May 2025, and four companion recommendations were published the same day: two ways of securing a credential, a status format for withdrawing one, and a controlled identifier document format. What it does not do is move a credential between two parties. No finished recommendation defines that exchange, and the specification only observes, in a section it marks non-normative, that its roles suggest where such protocols would go. Two things a standards audience should hold on to: it does not require decentralized identifiers, only web addresses, so the two families are often paired by habit rather than by rule; and selective disclosure is a property of the chosen securing mechanism, which means the issuer has to enable it at issuing time and the holder cannot add it later.

coverage.note: Defines the data model for a tamper-evident claim and the three roles of issuer, holder and checking party.

sources.title: Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0, W3C Recommendation 15 May 2025
sources.quote: This specification describes the extensible data model for verifiable credentials, how they can be secured from tampering, and a three-party ecosystem for the exchange of these credentials that is composed of issuers, holders, and verifiers.

coverage.note: Requires the issuing party to be named by a web address and recommends that the address resolve to a controlled identifier document; what is missing is any identifier system of its own, and decentralized identifiers appear only as one example among several.

coverage.note: A credential data model presents nothing and has no compositor.
Credentials are signed statements, not sensor streams; nothing in the model reads a face or a body pose.
No scene and no place, so no walkable surface or arrival point.
The model names claims about subjects, not published units of logic; a credential type is a vocabulary term, not an address for code.

A moderation decision could be carried as a credential, but the standard defines no review, no reviewer and no path from finished content to an audience, so the row is not what this specification is for.
No maps and no geometry in a credential data model.
No geographic area of application is expressed by the model itself.
The data model specifies context and type-based extensions with defined interpretation rules; new properties require the associated vocabulary rather than unstructured ad hoc parsing.
